blocks.text: **The problem.** Given two strings `haystack` and `needle`, return the index where `needle` first occurs in `haystack`, or `-1` if it doesn't occur at all. This is `indexOf` / `find` — and the question is how to write it yourself.

blocks.alt: Searching for ababca in abababca. On the first try, lined up at index 0, four letters match and then the fifth fails: the haystack has a where the needle has c. Instead of starting again one place to the right, the needle slides two places, because the four matched letters, abab, end with ab, which is also how the needle starts. Those two letters are already known to match, so the comparison carries on from the same haystack position, and the whole needle matches at index 2.

blocks.text: Many string questions come down to **where does this pattern occur in this text** — or to a fact about how a string's **beginning compares to its end**. The direct way lines the pattern up at every start and compares letter by letter. That is O(n · m) when there are many near-misses: looking for `"aaab"` in `"aaaaaaaa…"` matches three letters at every start before failing.

The **Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP)** algorithm finds the pattern in **O(n + m)** by never reading a text letter twice. It first studies the pattern on its own and builds a table: `lps[i]` is the length of the longest **border** of `pattern[0..i]` — a proper prefix that is also a suffix. In `"abab"`, the border is `"ab"`. After a mismatch with `j` letters matched, those `j` letters are known, and the longest border of them is already a matching start of the pattern. So `j` drops to `lps[j - 1]` and the text position stays put.

The table is built the same way, by matching the pattern against itself. When the next letter doesn't extend the current border, the next candidate is the **border of that border**, `lps[len - 1]`. The same table answers the next two lessons too: a string with a long border repeats itself, and a border of `s + "#" + reverse(s)` is a palindrome at the start of `s`.
In real code, use the built-in `indexOf` / `find` — but in an interview, expect to write the direct version first and explain KMP as the follow-up.
**Time O(n · m), space O(1).** Up to n - m + 1 starts, each comparing up to m letters. After a mismatch, the next start forgets everything the last one learned.

blocks.caption: Build the border table for the needle, then scan the haystack once without ever moving back.

blocks.text: **Time O(n + m), space O(m).** In the scan, every step either moves `i` forwards (at most n times) or makes `j` smaller — and `j` can't shrink more often than it grew, which is only when `i` moved. The table is built the same way in O(m).

rows.timeWhy: Up to **n − m + 1** starts, each comparing up to **m** letters.
Building the table is O(m); the scan **never re-reads** a text letter.
rows.spaceWhy: The `lps` table, **one entry per pattern letter**.

blocks.text: On ordinary text the brute force fails fast and is quick. KMP wins on repetitive inputs — DNA, binary data, or a test case built to be slow — where it stays linear no matter what.

items: **Needle longer than the haystack** — return `-1` without reading past the end.
**Match at the very end** — `"hello"` and `"llo"`: the last start to try is n - m, not n - m - 1.
**Repetitive input** — `"aaaaaaaab"` and `"aaab"`: the slow case for brute force.
**Off by one in the fall back** — after j matched letters it is `lps[j - 1]`, not `lps[j]`.
**Repeated Substring Pattern** — the same table tells whether a string is one block repeated. Next lesson.
**Shortest Palindrome** — KMP on `s + "#" + reverse(s)`. The lesson after.
**Rabin–Karp** — compare a rolling hash of each window instead of its letters: O(n + m) expected, and it handles many patterns of the same length at once (Repeated DNA Sequences).
**Z-algorithm** — another linear-time table, `z[i]` = how far the string starting at i matches its own start, with the same uses as KMP.
